name: Wine Red
lede: Wine Red is a dark, slightly bluish red named for the drink, and it has been in color charts for centuries, from Maerz and Paul to RAL.

sections.title: A name from the glass
sections.body: Paterson's dictionary defines wine red simply as a dark red, and lists a family of cousins: wine-colour, wine-dark, wine-gum red and wine yellow, which is a light reddish-yellow [1]. The point is darkness more than hue, as the article on [[red-wine]] explains. Neighbors on screen include [[burgundy]], [[claret]], [[carmine]] and [[oxblood]] [2].

sections.title: In the standards
sections.body: Maerz and Paul's 1930 dictionary has the color, and gives the first record as about 1750 [2]. The ISCC-NBS system of 1955 files it in block 13, and RAL has a wine red, RAL 3005, with an approximate screen value of #5E2028, much darker than this swatch [2]. The xkcd color survey has yet another wine red, #7B0323 [2]. So the phrase covers a family of dark reds, not one color [2].

sections.title: Red stones and red gowns
sections.body: The phrase also turns up in writing about materials. St Clair calls cinnabar, the principal ore of mercury, a wine-red stone, and the Romans prized its ground pigment, [[vermilion]] [3]. In the nineteenth-century handbook by Salter, quoted in the Compendium, a wine-red liquid appears in the preparation of a speculative pigment [4]. Gage points to a rich wine-red gown in Sassetta's panels about a saint's renunciation of his father, a color whose damage conservators studied [5].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: There are 55 paintings in our archive of 23,781 where this swatch covers at least five per cent of the canvas, within six color-distance units, among them Bronzino's portrait of Giovanni de' Medici (1545) [6]. The color is most over-represented in the 1300s through 1500s, at between 2.7 and 5.2 times its overall rate, and under-represented after 1600 [6]. These are photographs of aged, varnished paintings, so reds in particular are as photographed [6].
